catalog_quote: [Yeh 2016: 18, sec. 2.3.2 重音] 賽夏語重音一般落在詞的最後一個音節，加了-an、-en等後綴的詞亦適用此一重音規則，例如kaSa:engan[kasa:eŋán]「椅子」及kasi’aelen[kasi’ælʹən]「食物」，重音仍然落在最後一個音節。 [Tsuchida 1964: 43-44] A stress always falls on the final syllable of a word with a relatively high pitch, and thus it can be considered non-distinctive. The following words having a stress on the penult form exceptions: /bonaŋ/ "betel-nut" /kiŋkayni?/ "to dislike, don't like" It must be noted, however, that /bonaŋ/ is apparently a loan word from Amoy ... and that /kiŋkayni?/ is suspected to be further analizable into two morphemes. [Chiang & Chang-Liao 2004: 60] Pitch accent within words usually falls on the last syllable, except for function words and place names.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is fixed on the final (ultimate) syllable of content words; it is realized mainly by high F0 (Chiang & Chiang classify it as lexical pitch accent rather than stress), is non-contrastive, and marks the right word boundary. Function words and place names are exempt; Tsuchida lists two penult-accented lexical exceptions, one a Hokkien loan and one probably bimorphemic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in either open source.
new_statements.exceptions: Function words and place names (Chiang & Chang-Liao 2004: 60; Chiang & Chiang 2005: 405 citing Yeh 2000); penult accent in /bonaŋ/ 'betel-nut' (Amoy loan) and /kiŋkayni?/ 'dislike' (Tsuchida 1964: 43-44).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: Tsuchida defines the word as the minimal free form and (fn 7, after Chao Jung-lang) notes the stress marks a word boundary in compounds/numerals; Chiang & Chang-Liao measured citation-form words in short sentences, accented syllables 'invariably final' (p. 63). Both Northern (Wufeng) and Southern (Tungho/Nanzhuang) dialects: Tsuchida = Tungho (Southern); Chiang & Chang-Liao = one Northern + one Southern speaker. Chiang & Chiang 2005 argue the prominence is pitch accent (F0-cued), not duration/intensity stress; position (final) is agreed by all sources.
new_statements.identity_note: Saisiyat has two dialects, Northern (Wufeng, Hsinchu; Ta'ai) and Southern (Nanzhuang/Tungho, Miaoli). Tsuchida 1964 describes the Tungho (Southern) dialect; Chiang & Chang-Liao 2004 used one Northern and one Southern speaker; both report final accent, so the statement holds for sais1237 as a whole. Glottolog 5.1 lists no separate dialect glottocodes in the target record.

new_statements.quote: 賽夏語重音一般落在詞的最後一個音節，加了-an、-en等後綴的詞亦適用此一重音規則，例如kaSa:engan[kasa:eŋán]「椅子」及kasi’aelen[kasi’ælʹən]「食物」，重音仍然落在最後一個音節。 [p. 15:] 須注意的是，英語的/ə/不出現在重音節，而賽夏語的/ə/可出現在重音節，如sazek/sazək/「聞」中的/ə/即出現在重音所在的最後一個音節。
new_statements.translation: In Saisiyat, stress generally falls on the last syllable of the word; words that have taken suffixes such as -an and -en also follow this stress rule, e.g. kaSa:engan [kasa:eŋán] 'chair' and kasi'aelen [kasi'ælʹən] 'food', where the stress still falls on the last syllable. [p. 15:] Note that English /ə/ does not occur in stressed syllables, whereas Saisiyat /ə/ can occur in a stressed syllable; e.g. the /ə/ of sazek /sazək/ 'smell' occurs in the final syllable, where the stress is.

new_statements.relation_note: Same book as index 1 (printed 2016, Glottolog dates it 2018). The listed open_url host alilin.apc.gov.tw does not resolve (automated download (6), two attempts, https and http/IPv4); the identical book is open on alilin.cip.gov.tw (Book/399) and its full text layer was already held by the project; the live page-40 XML re-downloaded now is byte-identical to the on-disk copy. Final-syllable placement agrees with the catalog (fixed: final syllable) and with Tsuchida 1964 and Chiang & Chang-Liao 2004; adds that suffixed forms keep final stress and lists particle-level exceptions (ila, ay). Uses the term 重音 'stress', not pitch accent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the final syllable of the word; suffixes (-an, -en) are included in the domain, so stress shifts to the suffix. Schwa can bear it (no weight sensitivity mentioned).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 一般 'generally'. Elsewhere in the book: the new-situation aspect marker ila bears stress while the two-syllable 'ina does not (printed p. 97, ebook p. 119); the yes/no question particle ay raises the intonation and draws the stress of the preceding word onto itself (printed p. 151, ebook p. 173); emphasis lengthens the final vowel and raises pitch (printed p. 15).
new_statements.identity_note: Yeh 2016/2018 explicitly describes the 東河 (walo', Tungho) dialect, the Southern dialect centred in Nanzhuang, Miaoli (printed p. 4; dialect table p. 2). Tsuchida 1964 (already in the existing statements) also describes Tungho. Chiang & Chang-Liao 2004 had one Northern (Ta'ai) and one Southern speaker. No source read here reports a dialect difference in stress placement.
